fullAnalysis: Pinpoint #530 is one of those boards where the connector becomes obvious as soon as you stop searching for a category. Of, Golf, Main, Crash, and Stay the do not belong to one topic, but they all sound like incomplete expressions. That usually means the answer is a shared trailing word rather than a subject area.

My first instinct was to treat Golf and Main as the anchors because they are the easiest to complete. Golf course and main course both arrive immediately, which makes course a strong candidate. The real check is whether the rest of the board keeps working without strain. Of course is one of the most common phrases in English, crash course is the familiar label for an intensive introduction, and stay the course is the standard expression for continuing despite difficulty. Once all five land naturally, there is no reason to keep searching.

The board works because the same ending serves very different functions. Golf course names a place, main course names part of a meal, of course is conversational emphasis, crash course is an accelerated learning format, and stay the course is an idiom about persistence. That variety is exactly what makes phrase puzzles like this feel broader than they really are.
That is why the answer to LinkedIn Pinpoint #530 is Words that come before "course". The clues are not trying to form one thematic group. They are all waiting for the same final word.

lessons: When several clues feel half-finished, test a shared ending before you waste time hunting for a subject category.
Use the easiest phrase first. Golf course and main course make course a fast candidate, and the rest of the clues verify it.
